profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal planning meeting in a university ML-and-transportation lab to scope and assign work for a new review article tentatively titled "Deep Reinforcement Learning and Transportation Research: A Comprehensive Review — 2022-2025 Update and Resource Companion" for a Transportation Research Part C special issue on AI for mobility. The paper is intended to extend an earlier broad review by adding recent DRL transportation papers, updating the seven application categories, and including a practitioner-oriented appendix of implementation resources. The agenda is to decide the literature window, how the evidence table will be structured, what counts as a completed screening pass, how the resources appendix will be assembled, and who owns each deliverable. The expected outcome is an apparently shared plan for the search-and-coding workflow, division of labor, and a near-term milestone for an internal outline and master spreadsheet.

members.name: Dr. Lina Chen
members.expertise: Deep reinforcement learning for transportation systems, survey writing, traffic control applications
members.background: Leads a transportation ML lab and previously co-authored a tutorial-style DRL overview for civil engineering audiences; experienced in positioning review papers for transportation journals.
members.private_state: She wants a fast, publishable update that looks systematic without creating a large manual-verification burden, and she is worried that an overly ambitious workflow will delay submission to the special issue.
hidden_assumptions: In a review paper, the natural counting unit is one included article per row, even if a paper studies multiple transportation tasks.
"Screened" is satisfied once titles, abstracts, and metadata are deduplicated and tagged well enough to support category planning.
The "available resources" section should list simulators, repositories, and benchmark links reported by authors, not require testing whether they still run.
An update "since the last review" should begin from the previous review's search cutoff, including early-access papers around 2022 that the earlier synthesis would have missed.

members.name: Dr. Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Systematic literature reviews, reproducibility auditing, RL tooling and benchmark curation
members.background: Trained in computer science, has built benchmark spreadsheets and small reproduction checklists for RL papers, and recently joined the lab to strengthen its methodological rigor.
members.private_state: He wants the review to produce a durable dataset and resource appendix that other researchers can actually use, and he is concerned that paper-level aggregation will hide how DRL is adapted across distinct transportation settings.
hidden_assumptions: For a synthesis of applications, a "study" means each distinct transportation problem setting within a paper, not merely the paper itself.
"Screened" implies full-text extraction into a coding sheet with task, simulator, reward design, and training details captured.
A resources appendix is only genuinely useful if links are checked and basic compatibility with current tool versions is noted.
An update "since the last review" starts after the earlier review appeared publicly, which in practice means mostly 2023 onward rather than backfilling 2022 edge cases.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a 'study' in the master table
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to build a table of all included "studies" and mention totals like 120-150 studies.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means one row per paper/article, because inclusion and counting in review workflows are article-based.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means one row per distinct transportation application setting within a paper, such as separate entries for traffic signal control and ramp metering if both appear in the same article.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both interpretations are common in review writing, and the word "study" sounds precise enough that neither expects it to need unpacking during a planning meeting.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for the literature to be 'screened' by Friday
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the recent papers should be "screened" by Friday so they can look at category balance.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a deduplicated Zotero library with title/abstract tags and provisional category labels.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means full-text coding completed for the set, with fields populated in the extraction spreadsheet.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In systematic-review contexts, both light screening and full extraction are often discussed as progress milestones, and the Friday checkpoint is framed casually enough that the stricter criterion never gets surfaced.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to include an appendix of "available resources" for actually implementing DRL in transportation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the appendix will include citations and links to code repositories, simulators, and benchmark suites mentioned in the literature, regardless of current usability.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the appendix should include only resources that he has at least link-checked and lightly validated for present-day use, with notes on versions like SUMO 1.19 or RLlib 2.x compatibility.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are genuinely talking about resources for implementation, and the difference lies in invisible inclusion boundaries rather than in an overt disagreement about whether the appendix should exist.

misalignment_points.topic: The time window implied by 'since the last review'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly refer to covering papers published "since the last review."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes this means everything after the earlier review's search cutoff, including 2022 early-access and online-first papers that were not in the prior corpus.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes this means papers appearing after the earlier review was publicly available, effectively focusing on 2023-2025.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The earlier review is a shared reference point, so each assumes the boundary is obvious; the hidden divergence is about which date attached to that review matters operationally.

turns.inner_thought: This special issue is a good vehicle if we keep the update disciplined and not turn it into a giant reproducibility project. I want something that feels comprehensive and systematic, but still moves quickly. The resources appendix can add practical value without forcing us to test every repository or simulator; citing what the papers report should be enough for this venue.
turns.utterance: I think this special issue is a very good moment for us to do an updated comprehensive review, especially if we pair it with an appendix of available resources for actually implementing DRL in transportation. That combination should fit both the Part C audience and the tutorial-style expectation.

turns.inner_thought: Using the seven application categories gives continuity, but I want the update to be genuinely useful as a dataset. If we capture every relevant study since the last review, we can show how the same paper may treat multiple transportation problem settings differently. For me the window should really begin after the previous review was out in the world, so the bulk will be 2023 onward.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. We can use the earlier seven-category structure as the starting scaffold, then capture every relevant study since the last review and see whether the balance across categories has shifted enough to justify some refinements.

turns.inner_thought: If we count one included article per row, the corpus should stay manageable, probably around 120 to 150. That's enough to look substantial but not so large that screening and synthesis drag on for months. I really do not want us fragmenting multi-application papers into many entries and inflating the workload.
turns.utterance: My rough guess is that the update stays manageable if we're in the range of about 120 to 150 studies. If we keep the master table clean and consistent, that should be enough for a solid synthesis without making the paper unwieldy.

turns.inner_thought: I'll build the sheet so each distinct application setting is coded separately; otherwise the synthesis will blur together signal control, eco-driving, transit, and so on when they appear in the same article. Also, starting since the last review, I expect the post-publication wave to dominate anyway, so most of the work should be 2023-2025 papers. Lina's estimate sounds plausible if she's thinking more coarsely, but once coded at the study level the count may climb.
turns.utterance: I can set up the extraction sheet so the application-side coding stays clean, and I'll start from papers since the last review, which I suspect will make up most of the corpus anyway. That should give us a good early picture of where the volume is accumulating.

turns.inner_thought: I need a near-term checkpoint that is light enough to hit. By Friday, a deduplicated Zotero library with title, abstract, metadata tags, and provisional category labels would already let us judge category balance and draft the outline. We absolutely do not need full coding of every paper by then.
turns.utterance: Could we set a Friday milestone where the recent papers are screened and the category counts are visible enough that we can shape the outline? Even a clear first pass would help us decide how much space each section needs.

turns.inner_thought: Friday is tight but workable if I focus. For me, 'screened' should mean the full-text extraction is already entered for the initial set, at least for the biggest clusters, so the category balance rests on actual coding rather than metadata guesses. I'll prioritize traffic signal control and eco-driving because those are likely to dominate and reveal any coding issues early.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's doable. I'll treat Friday as the point by which the recent literature is screened, and I'll prioritize the traffic signal control and eco-driving clusters first so the category picture is informative right away.

turns.inner_thought: Good. Meanwhile the resources appendix can be built with relatively low effort by harvesting repository links, simulator names, and benchmark references from the included papers as they come in. That gives us a practitioner-facing deliverable without adding a lot of verification overhead.
turns.utterance: In parallel, I think we can assemble the available resources appendix as we go by pulling repository links, simulator names, and benchmark references from the included papers. That way the practical companion piece grows alongside the review rather than becoming a separate task at the end.

turns.inner_thought: That's exactly where I can add value. If the appendix is going to be genuinely useful, I should annotate whether links still work, whether environments install, and at least note current version issues like SUMO updates or RLlib changes. I won't say all that explicitly now because we're aligned on having the appendix, and I can just build the annotations into it.
turns.utterance: That works for me. As I pull those together, I can annotate the available resources so readers have a sense of which ones are still usable under current tool versions and which environments install cleanly.

turns.inner_thought: I'll keep ownership of the framing, mathematical background, and high-level synthesis, since that's where my prior review experience matters. Arjun can own the spreadsheet and coding for papers since the last review. In my mind that includes the 2022 online-first and early-access items missed by the previous review's search cutoff; I assume he'll naturally catch those once he searches comprehensively.
turns.utterance: Let's divide it this way: I'll take the mathematical background, the positioning against the earlier review, and the main synthesis sections. You own the coded spreadsheet for papers since the last review, plus the category breakdown that will feed the figures and appendix.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll circulate what I consider the screened spreadsheet: full-text coded entries for the post-review set, probably dominated by 2023 onward, with preliminary category counts at the study level. That should be enough to turn into a serious outline and maybe expose where we need a few more targeted searches.
